passage:
Lights-out at the residential school hostel was at ten, but Naveen was still under his torch with a physics workbook. Baljeet leaned over from the top bunk.
'You're always saying whatever is written will happen. So why kill yourself over numericals?'
Naveen smiled without looking up. 'My Dadi says the pen is ours and the page is God's.' He underlined a formula. 'I do my part. The rest isn't mine to fret over.'
'And last year? When you missed the science olympiad by one mark?'
Naveen was quiet a moment. 'I cried that night. Then I thought, maybe it wasn't meant to be that year. It let me sleep. But I still went back and found the mark I lost.'
Baljeet flopped back onto the pillow. 'Weird. But it works for you.'

qa.q: By how many marks did Naveen miss the science olympiad?
What did Naveen feel the night he missed the olympiad, and what brought him peace?
qa.a: He was upset enough to cry, and the thought that it wasn't meant to be that year calmed him enough to sleep.

qa.q: What choice did Naveen make after that loss that kept the work in his own hands?
qa.a: He went back and found the mark he lost, so his belief in fate comforted him without stopping him from improving.

qa.q: How does Baljeet see Naveen's way of holding fate and effort together?
qa.a: Baljeet finds it odd, even contradictory, at first, but admits it seems to work for Naveen.

grounding: Shows a teenager from a traditional home who trusts destiny, finds peace after a loss through it, and still studies hard and owns his part.

passage:
Dear Ankita Didi,
The water has gone down now. We lost most of the stock in the shop: the rice sacks, the notebooks, even Baba's old ledger. Ma sat on the steps that first evening and said, 'What was written, was written.' I thought she would be broken, but she seemed almost peaceful, and somehow that made me calm too.
I believe that as well, Didi. Some things come from above. But the boards are in March, and nobody above is going to learn trigonometry for me. So I study at the neighbour's house in the mornings and help Baba sort the dry stock in the evenings.
The flood took the shop's goods. It didn't take my pencil.
Write soon,
Binita

qa.q: What did the family lose when the water came?
qa.a: Most of the stock in the shop: the rice sacks, the notebooks and even Baba's old ledger.

qa.q: Why did Binita feel calm after the flood?
qa.a: Seeing Ma almost peaceful, trusting that what was written was written, helped Binita feel calm as well.

qa.q: What choice did Binita make that kept both faith and effort alive?
qa.a: Binita chose to study at the neighbour's house in the mornings and help Baba in the evenings, accepting the loss without leaving the boards to fate.

qa.q: How might Ankita Didi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: She might feel relieved that Binita is coping calmly and proud of the steady studying, while also sad about the family's losses.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose family's belief in fate brings peace after a loss, while the teenager keeps taking responsibility for studying.
